title: Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time
authors: Spiering BA, Mujika I, Sharp MA, Foulis SA
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: General populations (endurance and strength training studies); insufficient data for athletes or military personnel
findings: In general populations, endurance performance can be maintained for up to 15 weeks when training frequency is cut to as few as 2 sessions per week or exercise volume is cut by 33-66% (as low as 13-26 minutes per session), provided exercise intensity (exercising heart rate) is maintained.

Strength and muscle size (at least in younger people) can be maintained for up to 32 weeks with as little as 1 strength session per week and 1 set per exercise at maintained relative load; older people may need up to 2 sessions and 2-3 sets per exercise.
Exercise intensity seems to be the key variable for maintaining performance despite large reductions in frequency and volume.
Insufficient data exist for specific recommendations for athletes or military personnel.
limitations: Brief narrative review of mostly short studies in non-athletes; not specific to long-distance running; the 15-week figure is a bound set by study durations, not a safe limit; the 'or' between frequency and volume reductions means the combination is not shown.
implications: Implement a time-limited maintenance mode: about 2 runs per week, weekly volume cut 33-66% (sessions of at least 13-26 min), at least one session at usual intensity, and 1 strength session per week at 1 set per exercise (2 sessions and 2-3 sets for older runners).
Default maintenance mode to at most about 15 weeks, then re-check fitness; do not apply it to 50 km-100 mile fitness without a caveat that ultra-specific durability is not covered.
